Last month U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins announced plans for a major reorganization of the U.S. Forest Service.  

I talked about the Forest Service reorganization and why it matters last month with my friend, Wisconsin native Mike Dombeck.  In a career in conservation that started as a teenager guiding musky fishing clients in Hayward, Mike went onto a long career in public lands that included serving as the Forest Service Chief from 1997 until 2001.  

The U.S. Forest Service has a long proud history with origins under President Teddy Roosevelt. The Forest Service today manages more than 193 million acres of our National Forests and Grasslands, including the more than 1.5 Million acre Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest here in Wisconsin. The Forest Service is the largest federal wildfire response agency, leads the world’s largest natural resources research agency, and supports state and local agencies involved in forest management and caring for trees in our cities.  

The recently proposed Forest Service reorganization, along with the President’s proposed 2027 budget for the Forest Service and his recent Executive Orders would all result in an agency severely reduced in scope, capacity, and funding.  Simply put, the Forest Service and its dedicated career professionals won’t be able to adequately care for our forests and all the benefits they provide if this reorganization goes through.      

This kind of reorganization was also explicitly prohibited without Congressional approval as recently as November 2025 with language in the USDA Appropriations bill.  And yet again, this Congress is sitting back, watching another agency decimated by the Project 2025 agenda.    

We’ll share my conversations with Mike recorded at his home near Stevens Point in four segments over the next few weeks.  This is segment #1.
